messages.subject_clean: Negative Binomial, K, and model inference
messages.body_plain:
I have repeated count data (1-6 surveys of 195 sites, where 155 sites have 5 surveys). Unfortunately, using an N-mixture model with a Poisson distribution leads to a poor fitting model. A zip model doesn't fair much/any better. When comparing models with AIC the Negative Binomial model does by far the best. However, as pointed out in previous discussions, the negative binomial can help improve overdispersed counts but can be problematic because of the exceedingly long tail. In my case, the estimates of N[i] for some sites continue to increase with increasing K (subset of estimates where K = 1000 and original data):

Even if I remove all the sites with NA the results are similar. On a 100 sq m site where we saw 17-52 salamanders per survey the BUP mode is 890. There might be 900 salamanders in that area including all species but certainly not of just one species. I guess my question is more philosophical. Do people think it would be better to truncate the NB by setting K to some max value of N[i] so that some overdispersion is allowed that is not accounted for by covariates or would it be better to use a Poisson and ZIP model that don't have great fit? I tried a Poisson-lognormal in WinBUGS but didn't get convergence no matter what I tried. It seems like part of the story will be that there is unaccounted for variation (in detection primarily?) that we are not able to model despite using many covariates and many combinations generally thought to influence salamander activity. When we do assume a Poisson distribution, the estimated abundance is not very different from the max count at a given site (often 10x less than NB estimate). Should I just use this model and say in publication that the negative binomial gave unrealistic abundance values and was no longer considered as a viable model despite much lower AIC (that's what I plan to do now)? Either way it seems like I will be describing models with poor fit based on Chi sq or SSE metrics.

This brings up the question of whether a Negative Binomial is ever useful when counts are high (>10)? Will the long tail always cause a problem like this, especially with the 97% CI? Below is other information that I've gathered from previous unmarked discussions and from Kery et al. 2005. Any suggestions would be appreciated as well as an discussion about use of the negative binomial, setting K, or model inference.

Thanks,
Dan

Andy:

My belief is that you probably want to set K high enough so that
there's no affect at all on the MLE -- when I wrote "possible values"
what I meant was mathematically possible, i.e., the support of the
random variable N, not biological possible.

An interesting example arises when you consider the negative binomial
model. For some reason ecologists are obsessed about fitting negative
binomial models (there are now dozens of papers). For the NB model
there is extreme sensitivity to the value of K for these models owing
to, essentially, a very long right tail of the negative binomial
model. You will find in many practical situations that you need to use
K=several hundred (even 1000) to realize no effect on the MLEs. So, NB
models imply support for N on extremely large and unreasonable
(biologically) values.

choosing a value of N that truncates the likelihood is effectively
like using an informative prior distribution which seems to be
generally frowned about in the literature.  You would have to argue
that N=10 makes sense (or whatever), and someone else might think N=8
makes sense, and you find that everyone has their own answer!

regards
andy

Richard:

What are your estimates of lambda, p, and alpha from the "null" negative binomial model? I might expect strange behavior if p is very low and alpha is very high. Notice that K doesn't have much influence on "good" data once K is high enough.

 Andy:

Sometimes the NB model is very unstable, when either the data set is relatively sparse or when extreme over-dispersion is indicated. We had some cases of this in the Kery et al. 2005 paper (Ecol. Apps). What happens, I think, is that excessive over-dispersion can look like really low encounter probability (among other things) and this induces a near-nonidentifiability problem -- but also MLEs that occur near p=0 which causes E[N] to be huge also. Caution is in order whenever fitting the NB model.

Kery et al. 2005

Nevertheless, the negative binomial distribution may not always be an ideal choice for representing the overdispersion in abundance relative to the Poisson. We feel that the mean/variance relationship implied by the negative binomial model may be extreme, and this has an especially deleterious effect on estimation for highly abundant species and those for which considerable variation is indicated. In such cases, the model fits the high mean and accommodates low counts by inflating the variance, yielding a strongly right-skewed abundance distribution that places considerable mass at excessive, and perhaps unrealistic, values of abundance.

Other random-effects distributions may be adopted for abundance that may prove adequate for describing overdispersion and may provide more stable maximum likelihood estimates than the negative binomial. We considered finite mixtures of Poisson distributions with some success. We also have briefly investigated the uniform-integrated Poisson (Bhattacharya and Holla1965) and Generalized Hermite distributions (Puig 2003), but have not developed adequate experience with these at this time (J. A. Royle, unpublished data). More work on comparing different kinds of mixtures will be beneficial.

Variation in abundance may be accommodated implicitly as overdispersion, such as by the negative bi- nomial distribution, or explicitly by modeling covariates into the mean. Although binomial mixture models worked well both for species with fairly restricted range and for those that are widespread (representing small and large sample sizes), we encountered some numerical problems for two extreme data sets (Hawfinch and Coal Tit). With more informative explanatory variables, it is likely that improvements could be achieved.

hi Kathi,
Disclaimer: I've never used pcountOpen() so I can't say exactly what is
the problem here.
However, I believe the structure you have for "yearlySiteCovs" looks
right (one column for each year). If you have obsCovs then I think they
would be the same number of columns as "years x reps". So if you have 2
years with 3 reps then you would need 6 columns on that matrix. There was
this example from Richard's ALFL data:

library(unmarked)
alfl.umf <- unmarkedFramePCO(y=alfl.data[,1:6],
siteCovs=alfl.data[,c("woody", "struct")],
# we could have yearlySiteCovs here.
obsCovs=list(time=alfl.data[,c("time1_05", "time2_05", "time3_05",
"time2_06", "time3_06", "time3_06")],
date=alfl.data[,c("date1_05", "date2_05", "date3_05",
"date2_06", "date3_06", "date3_06")]),
numPrimary=2)

Ok, so I don't think this helps you solve your problem. Is it possible
that one of your covariates is a factor with only a single level?
I suggest the following process to obtain more information:
(1) get rid of all the yearlySiteCovs and see if it runs
(2) add the covariates one at a time and see if it crashes on a specific
one.
(3) Look at the structure of that covariate and make sure things are
right.

regards,
andy

I think the problem is that p must be very very low in your case, and when p is extremely low, then abundance estimates will be very high, which I think is what you are seeing. Richard

> An interesting example arises when you consider the negative binomial
> model. For some reason ecologists are obsessed about fitting negative

> there is extreme sensitivity to the value of K for these models owing
> to, essentially, a very long right tail of the negative binomial
> model. You will find in many practical situations that you need to use
> K=several hundred (even 1000) to realize no effect on the MLEs. So, NB
> models imply support for N on extremely large and unreasonable
> (biologically) values.
>
> choosing a value of N that truncates the likelihood is effectively
> like using an informative prior distribution which seems to be
> generally frowned about in the literature.  You would have to argue
> that N=10 makes sense (or whatever), and someone else might think N=8
> makes sense, and you find that everyone has their own answer!
>

> andy
>
>

>

>

Apps). What happens, I think, is that excessive over-dispersion can look like really low encounter probability (among other things) and this induces a near-nonidentifiability problem -- but also MLEs that occur near p=0 which causes E[N] to be huge also. Caution is in order whenever fitting the NB model.
>
>
>
> Kery et al. 2005
>
> Nevertheless, the negative binomial distribution may not always be an ideal choice for representing the overdispersion in abundance relative to the Poisson. We feel that the mean/variance relationship implied by the negative binomial model may be extreme, and this has an especially deleterious effect on estimation for highly abundant species and those for which considerable variation is indicated. In such cases, the model fits the high mean and accommodates low counts by inflating the variance, yielding a strongly right-skewed abundance distribution that places considerable mass at excessive, and perhaps unrealistic, values of abundance.

>

With more informative explanatory variables, it is likely that improvements could be achieved.
>

messages.subject: Re: Structuring Missing Data
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the replies,

I have been in contact with Richard off-list and he provided the following comments:

"Basically, anytime you have a NA in an obsCov, the
corresponding "y" value needs to be removed. This is because there is
no likelihood contribution for such an observation. The warning message you see
is just telling you this. It isn't a problem except when you have covariates
with different patterns of missing values. In such a case, you need to ensure
that the missing values are consistent among covariates if you want to compare
them using AIC. This isn't an unmarked issue, it is an issue related to the use
of AIC in general."

In regards to imputing the missing obs-level covariates, Richard advised against this:

"I don't think that imputing (making up) values for the
missing observations is a good idea. But if you do it, you should assess how
sensitive the results are to different made-up values."

Cheers,
Dan

Dear Courtney,

offlist I send you code for a 4-level nested ANOVA according to Gelman (2006) and the Ecology paper by Qian and Shen (2007). You can see there how they code this. I am not sure about the plot effects in your code. I think I would also treat them as random effects in the analysis.

The other thing I was wondering about is why you don't use the density estimates with their SEs directly in a Normal mixed model ? From what I understand you do a two-step hierarchical model, with the distance sampling analysis coming first and then in the second step, you do stats on stats. So to propagate the uncertainty in the plot density estimates you could use both the density point estimates and their uncertainty (SE) as shown (with code given) in the JAPPL paper by McCarthy & Masters. Link and Sauer (Ecology, 2002, hierarchical model for trends of many species) have also done the same thing.

Re. testing for plot or transect effects, I think the DIC could work -- From what I understand, you should not believe the DIC for mixture models (e.g., Nmix or site-occ), but when all your random effects are continuous, that's probably OK.

# transects were randomly selected within larger 10km x 10km plots in an area
# looking for potential spatial correlation in counts at the transect and plot level
# Here the simulated data are just to show you the format - they're not explicitly spatially correlated

set.seed(4321)
# LEVEL 1
# sites
nsites<- 1000
# site level covariate
habitat<-rnorm(nsites) # a covariate value
# relationship between habitat and count
lambda<- exp(0.3 + .5*habitat)
C<-rpois(nsites,lambda) # site-specific counts
# LEVEL 2
# transects
ntran<-169
# transect id for each site
transect<-as.integer(seq(1,169,length.out=1000))

# there is probably a much better way to do this
# LEVEL 3
# plots

# plot id for each site

    model {

    # LEVEL 3

    #Prior distributions for random effect of plot

    for (p in 1:nplot){  # loop over all plots
    alpha.plot[p] ~ dnorm(alpha.over,tau.plot)   # plot effect -  contains overall alpha
    }
    # Fixed level 3 priors
    sd.plot ~ dunif(0,10)
    tau.plot <- pow(sd.plot,-2)
    alpha.over ~ dnorm(0,0.001)  # fixed overall intercept

    # LEVEL 2

Looks good to me except that I think you need a plot effect as well in the line with the linear predictor. I would change the line to something like:

log(lambda[i])<- alpha.tran[transect[i]] + alpha.plot[plot[i]] + beta1*habitat[i] # for likelihood - intercept is based on random

BTW, the way you had it, this would be centered on zero, because the overall mean is in the prior for the plot effects.

And you could also add a random point effect, to account for overdispersion relative to the Poisson. But perhaps that might be too much ?

Regards  --  Marc

andy

messages.body_plain:
Courtney,

Have you seen Chelgren et al. (2011) Herpetological Conservation and Biology?
 They have WinBUGS code for distance sampling that seems to work well.
They calculate the likelihood of sigma in a half-normal model based on
the individual distances, and then use that sigma to compute a capture
probability for individuals within the effective area of sampling.  That
 capture probability would then obviously be "pcap" in your model, but
otherwise your general model structure would be unchanged.

-Dan
